title: 2026 Korea Winter Guide: Skiing, Ice Festivals & Street Food
description: Your ultimate guide to winter in Korea (2026)! Discover ski resorts near Seoul, thrilling ice festivals, and must-try warm street food to beat the cold.

Skiing near Seoul: Hit the slopes without the epic travel time

Okay, so you wanna do a ski trip in Korea but dreading a flight to Gangwon-do? Ngl, it's a mood. But good news! There are actually some decent spots super close to Seoul that are totally doable for a weekend or even a day trip. You just gotta pick the right one. The vibe is mostly beginner-to-intermediate, so don't expect crazy expert terrain, but for shredding some powder and getting that Insta shot, they're perfect.

Jisan Forest Resort

Mapo Station (Gyeongui-Jungang Line) → Walk to Mapo Bus Station → Bus 1122 to Jisan Forest Resort. Opens 9:00 AM, Closes 5:00 AM (yes, really). This place is probably the most popular for Seoul day-trippers. It's got a good mix of slopes, and honestly, the rental gear is usually pretty solid. Plus, they have night skiing if you're feeling ambitious. Gets crowded, especially on weekends, so go early or brace yourself.

Star Hill Resort

Gondola Station, Hanam City. Not super easy via public transport tbh, closest is probably Gangdong-gu Office Station (Line 5) then a taxi. Open 9:00 AM - 10:00 PM daily. This one's smaller but has a chiller vibe. Good if you're a total beginner or just wanna mess around for a few hours. Less pressure, less chaos.

Must-See Ice Festivals: Frozen fun

Korea knows how to do winter festivals. They get seriously creative with the ice. These aren't just pretty; they're legit experiences. Bundle up, folks.

Hwacheon Sancheoneo Ice Festival (San isthe literal name of the fish, not a typo)

Hwacheon Station (Gyeongchun Line), then taxi. Usually late Jan-early Feb. This is THE big one. Think thousands of people fishing for mountain trout through holes in the ice. It's wild. There's also sledding, ice sculptures, and yeah, you can eat your catch. Cold? Yes. Worth it? Completely worth it. Just wear like, 5 layers.

Inje Ice Fishing Festival

Nearest major station: Chuncheon Station (Gyeongchun Line), then shuttle bus or taxi. Typically early February. Similar to Hwacheon, focuses on ice fishing (for trout again) but also has snow slides and cultural events. It's a bit more low-key than Hwacheon but still a solid winter fest experience.

Warm Up: Essential Winter Street Food

Okay, the ice is cool (literally), but you're gonna get cold. This is where Korean street food saves lives. Forget fancy restaurants, this is the real deal. Hit up a busy market or subway station exit, and you'll find these vendors.

Bungeoppang (붕어빵)

Fish-shaped pastries, usually filled with sweet red bean paste. They're cheap (like ₩1000 for 3 sometimes!) and piping hot. The crispy edges and warm, sweet filling? Chef's kiss. Pro tip: Sometimes you can find ones with custard or chocolate filling, keep an eye out.

Hotteok (호떡)

A sweet pancake, often filled with brown sugar, cinnamon, and nuts, then fried. Crispy outside, gooey inside. Absolute lifesaver on a freezing day. Some vendors also do savory versions now, but the classic sweet one is unbeatable.

Eomuk (어묵) / Odeng (오뎅)

Fish cakes on skewers, served in a hot broth. You'll find these EVERYWHERE. Grab a skewer, sip the broth – it's surprisingly flavorful and super warming. Usually around ₩1000 per skewer. It's the ultimate quick fix when you're freezing waiting for the subway.

Gyeranppang (계란빵)

Sweet and savory muffin-like bread with a whole egg baked inside. Sounds weird, tastes amazing. It’s moist, a little sweet, and the egg makes it surprisingly filling. Perfect snack while walking around.

Navigating Winter Travel

It's cold, yeah, but Korea handles winter surprisingly well. Public transport usually runs on time, even with snow. The biggest hassle is just staying warm. Layers are key. Think thermal base layers, a good fleece or down jacket, scarf, gloves, and a beanie. Seriously, don't skimp on the accessories.

If you're planning a ski trip or hitting up multiple festivals, mapping out your transit can save you a ton of hassle. Sites like CocoTrip's AI planner can help map out routes with transit times and even suggest accommodations near resorts, which is super useful if you're not fluent in Korean.

FAQ

Q. How much does a ski lift ticket cost in Korea?
A. Lift tickets can range from ₩50,000 to ₩90,000 for a full day, depending on the resort and day of the week. Rentals are extra, usually around ₩20,000-₩30,000.

Q. Are the ice fishing festivals hard to get to?
A. They require a bit of effort, usually involving a train to a nearby city and then a taxi or shuttle bus. Factor in travel time; it's often a full-day trip from Seoul.

Q. Can I find halal or vegan street food in winter?
A. It's tough. Most classic winter street foods (like hotteok, bungeoppang, eomuk) are not vegan. While you might find some vendors offering veggie options, it's rare. Look for dedicated halal/vegan restaurants in major cities like Seoul, especially near tourist areas. Planning ahead with a resource like CocoTrip's halal guide is recommended.

Q. What's the best way to travel between cities in winter?
A. The KTX high-speed train is usually the most efficient and comfortable way to travel between major cities like Seoul and Busan. Buses are also an option but can be slower in bad weather.
